title: True / False / Not Given
overview: Determine whether statements agree with factual claims in the passage (TRUE), directly contradict them (FALSE), or lack enough evidence to confirm or deny (NOT GIVEN).
strategies: Underline qualifiers such as 'all', 'exclusively', 'primarily', or 'before 2005'—these are frequent FALSE traps.
Never import outside knowledge; judge strictly against the exact passage sentence.
Answers almost always appear in sequential order through the text.

example.excerpt: When Toronto enacted its mandatory Green Roof Bylaw in 2009, hydrologists recorded up to 70 percent retention of summer rainfall.
example.statement: Toronto introduced voluntary green roof guidelines before 2000.
example.why: The text confirms mandatory bylaws began in 2009, but gives no information on whether voluntary guidelines existed before 2000.

practice.q: Passage: 'Harrison's H4 lost merely five seconds over eighty-one days.' Statement: H4 gained five seconds on its transatlantic voyage.
Passage: 'Watchmakers such as Larcum Kendall simplified H4 for mass naval production.' Statement: Larcum Kendall had previously studied astronomy in Greenwich.
practice.explanation: No biographical details about Kendall's prior study appear.

title: Matching Headings
overview: Select the heading that best captures the central idea of an entire paragraph rather than a single supporting detail.
strategies: Read the first two sentences and final concluding sentence of the paragraph before checking the heading list.
Eliminate headings that merely echo a single example inside the middle of the paragraph.
Cross out used headings carefully since there are always extra distractors.

example.excerpt: Paragraph D explains how saturated substrates weigh up to 350 kg/m2, forcing older warehouses into expensive steel upgrades or cheaper reflective paint.
example.correctAnswer: Engineering and cost obstacles to retrofitting
example.why: Both weight limits and financial trade-offs reflect retrofit barriers.

practice.q: Which sentence position most reliably reveals a paragraph's main purpose for Matching Headings?
practice.explanation: Academic paragraphs frame their thesis at the opening and wrap up implications at the end.

title: Multiple Choice & Distractor Traps
overview: Identify correct choices when speakers mention all three options before modifying, rejecting, or correcting one.
strategies: Listen for pivot words like 'however', 'actually', 'originally we planned', or 'that turned out to be full'.
Read question stems before audio starts; leave options light until the speaker narrows them.
Match synonyms rather than waiting for exact option wording.

example.excerpt: Speaker: 'We budgeted £35 initially, though summer demand pushed the refundable deposit to £45.'
example.why: £35 is a classic chronological distractor corrected by 'pushed... to £45'.

practice.q: Audio: 'The herbarium wasn't moved to the North Gate after all; you'll find it inside the West Pavilion.' Where is the herbarium?
practice.explanation: 'Wasn't moved... after all' rejects North Gate.

title: Plan & Map Labelling
overview: Follow spatial instructions, compass bearings, and relative prepositions ('adjacent to', 'diagonally across') on a visual floorplan.
strategies: Locate the 'You Are Here' starting arrow and check N/S/E/W compass orientation first.
Trace your pencil along the described path in real time so you stay synchronised.

example.excerpt: 'Proceed past the fountain; the cafe sits to your immediate left before the pond.'
example.why: Sequence markers ('past', 'before') anchor exact box labels.

practice.q: If a guide faces North and says 'turn right toward the east wing', which compass edge are you moving toward?
practice.explanation: Facing North puts East directly to your right.

title: Academic Task 1: Data Overview & Grouping
overview: Synthesise charts, tables, maps, or process diagrams in 150+ words with an explicit high-level overview and selective numerical comparisons.
strategies: Always write a distinct Overview paragraph summarising 2–3 headline patterns without listing raw minutiae.
Never invent reasons or outside speculation explaining why numbers changed.
Group body paragraphs logically by magnitude, trend direction, or time split.

example.excerpt: East Asia rose from 58 GW to 240 GW while South America climbed from 18 GW to 82 GW.
example.correctAnswer: Overall, every region expanded capacity substantially, with East Asia maintaining the largest scale throughout.
example.why: Captures general direction and clear leader without listing every figure.

practice.q: What is the single most common reason Academic Task 1 reports cap at Band 5.5?
practice.explanation: Official IELTS descriptors require a clear overview for Band 6+ and 7+ Task Achievement.

title: Task 2: Essay Structures (Opinion / Discussion)
overview: Develop a clear thesis supported by well-extended topic sentences, causal explanations, and concrete examples in 250+ words.
strategies: Spend 4 minutes outlining two clear central claims before typing a single word.
Ensure every body paragraph follows: Topic Sentence -> Explanation -> Illustration -> Mini-link.
Respond to ALL parts of two-part or 'discuss both views + opinion' prompts.

example.excerpt: Prompt: Discuss both views and give your opinion.
example.correctAnswer: Intro (both views + thesis) -> Body 1 (View A) -> Body 2 (View B + preference) -> Conclusion
example.why: Demonstrates clear progression and balanced coverage.

practice.q: In a 'Discuss both views and give your own opinion' essay, where should your personal opinion appear?
options: Thesis statement and conclusion (plus evaluation in body)
practice.answer: Thesis statement and conclusion (plus evaluation in body)
practice.explanation: A clear position throughout the response is essential for Band 7+ Task Response.

title: Speaking Part 2: 2-Minute Cue Card Storytelling
overview: Use 60 seconds of preparation notes to deliver a cohesive 1.5–2 minute narrative covering Past context, Present detail, and Personal reflection.
strategies: Write 4–6 keyword triggers during the 1-minute prep, never full sentences.
Use Past -> Detail -> Emotion -> Reflection timing so you comfortably reach the 2-minute mark.

example.excerpt: Cue card: Describe an impressive building.
example.correctAnswer: 'One architectural space that genuinely stood out to me is...'
example.why: Signals fluent natural lexical control immediately.

practice.q: How long do examiners give you to make notes before Speaking Part 2?
practice.explanation: IELTS allocates exactly 60 seconds of preparation time with pencil and paper.

title: Speaking Part 3: Abstract Discussion & Speculation
overview: Answer analytical, societal, and future-oriented questions beyond personal anecdotes using hedging and balanced comparison.
strategies: Shift from 'I think' to societal perspectives ('From a municipal standpoint...', 'On a broader scale...').
Give 3–5 sentence structured answers: Direct answer -> Why -> Example/Contrast.

example.excerpt: How might urban architecture evolve by 2050?
example.correctAnswer: 'It seems increasingly likely that cities will prioritise adaptive reuse and passive thermal facades...'
example.why: Uses natural speculation and topic-specific lexis.

practice.q: Which answer style works best in Speaking Part 3?
practice.explanation: Part 3 evaluates abstract reasoning and extended discourse.
